_status: Faults + error-code catalogue for the Part Finder. Curated from public sources; refine as you test. Code meanings can vary by control-board platform/generation.
_sources: Baumatic is owned by Candy (Haier Europe) — shares the Candy/Hoover Cuore platform

_schema.faults: applianceType -> faultId -> { label, synonyms[], components[] (ordered: most likely / check-first component first) }
_schema.note: components are search keywords/part-category terms, ranked by what an engineer would check/replace first. Every faultId used in errorCodes must exist in faults for that applianceType.

not-draining.label: Not draining / won't empty
discriminators: If you can HEAR THE PUMP HUMMING/straining but little or no water leaves, the drain pump is blocked or failing (or the filter/hose is blocked). Prioritise this over the motor even if it also won't spin - it won't spin until it has drained.
Won't drain AND won't spin: almost always the drain pump or a blocked pump filter (the machine won't spin until it has drained).
Drains slowly or noisily: partial blockage in the filter, or a worn pump impeller.
Drains fine but won't spin: this is NOT a drain fault - see motor/brushes/belt (motor-drum).

inlet-valve.label: Fill / water inlet fault (incl. overfill)
synonyms: fills with water when switched off
discriminators: A machine that FILLS with water while switched OFF is a water inlet valve stuck/not closing (mains pressure passes the failed valve) - route to the inlet valve; the anti-flood may trigger as a knock-on effect.
A loud buzz/hum only while FILLING is usually a restricted inlet (blocked inlet filter/kinked hose making the valve strain) or a failing water inlet valve. Check/clean the inlet filter first.

pressure-switch.label: Pressure switch / water level fault
synonyms: fills then drains over and over
discriminators: Repeatedly filling then draining over and over = the machine can't sense the water level, so it keeps correcting. Usual cause is a faulty pressure switch/sensor or a blocked/split pressure chamber (air-trap) hose.

heater.label: Heater / heating fault
discriminators: Washes but stays cold / long cycles: heater element or the NTC temperature sensor.
Trips the electrics when it should heat: heater element earthing/shorting.

door-lock.label: Door lock / interlock fault
synonyms: nothing happens when i press start
discriminators: A door that stays LOCKED after a cycle was interrupted or didn't finish is usually a CONSEQUENCE of the cycle not completing (often a drain or heater fault leaving it mid-programme) - not a failed lock. Only suspect the lock itself if the cycle completed normally but the door still won't release, or it won't lock to start.

Won't start when you press start: if it STILL HAS power/lights, the usual cause is the door interlock not confirming the door is shut (or a failed door lock / start switch). If it's COMPLETELY DEAD with no lights, look at the mains/fuse or PCB instead (main-pcb).

motor-drum.label: Motor / drum fault
discriminators: NOISE BY TIMING: a noise ONLY while DRAINING is the drain pump (see not-draining), not the drum. Motor can be heard but the drum doesn't turn = drive belt. Drum jerks / struggles to reach speed = motor or control/inverter (carbon brushes on brushed motors). Grinding/rumbling that worsens at high-speed spin = drum bearings.

A screech/squeal on spin = drum bearings or a glazed/slipping drive belt, NOT carbon brushes. A burning-rubber smell = a slipping/perished drive belt or a seized pump/motor - unplug it if the smell is strong.
Won't spin but drains fine and the drum turns freely by hand: carbon brushes (brushed motors) or a snapped/slipped drive belt.
Won't spin because water is left in the drum: it's a drain fault first (not-draining), not the motor.
Loud grinding/rumbling on spin with drum movement: drum bearings.
Brushless brands (LG/Samsung, newer Bosch): no carbon brushes - suspect the hall sensor or inverter PCB.

main-pcb.label: Control board / PCB fault (incl. EEPROM/config)
discriminators: If it went 'dead'/stuck RIGHT AFTER washing a single bulky, water-absorbent item (bath mat, rug, towels, duvet), that's almost certainly an unbalanced load, not this - the machine is stalled trying to rebalance. Redistribute/add smaller items and re-run before suspecting a part (see unbalanced-load).

leak-flood.label: Water leak / anti-flood (water in the base)
discriminators: A DARK, greasy/oily leak (not clear water) usually means the DRUM BEARINGS have failed - the bearing seal lets water past and dark residue out - or an oil-filled shock absorber is leaking. Listen for a grinding/rumbling on spin (bearings). Do NOT tell the customer the machine has no oil; front-loaders do have greased bearings and oil-damped absorbers. Clear-water leaks are the door seal, sump hose, pump or inlet valve.

Only say the anti-flood/Aquastop has TRIGGERED if the customer actually reports water in the base tray, a machine that has locked with a flood warning, or an anti-flood/LE/LC code - not for a plain 'it's leaking'.
If the customer can say WHERE the water appears (front/door, drawer, underneath, rear) or WHEN (fill, wash, drain/spin), use the matching leak-source node for a more specific diagnosis.

leak-door.label: Leak from the door / front
components: check the door seal folds for trapped debris or coins
discriminators: Front/door leaks: FIRST check the rubber door seal (boot) folds for a trapped item (coin, wire, debris) and wipe them clean - a free fix. Only replace the boot if it is genuinely torn, split or perished.
Water running down the front can also come from the detergent drawer above - check the drawer if the seal looks intact.

leak-dispenser.label: Leak from the detergent drawer
synonyms: water backs up out of the drawer
components: clean the detergent drawer and dispenser channels
discriminators: Drawer leaks are usually blocked/residue-clogged dispenser channels or too much detergent (oversudsing) pushing water out during fill - clean the drawer and channels and reduce the dose FIRST (free).
If the drawer is clean and it still leaks on fill, suspect the dispenser-to-tub hose or a slow-closing inlet valve.

leak-drain.label: Leak underneath / while draining (pump, filter or sump hose)
components: check the pump filter cap is seated and its seal is clean
discriminators: A leak underneath, or during drain/spin, is usually the pump filter cap not seated / its seal, the sump hose (tub-to-pump), or the drain pump housing - check the filter cap seating and seal FIRST (free) before replacing a part.
If the water only appears at the REAR during drain, it is often the external drain/waste hose connection rather than an internal part.
A dark, greasy/oily leak underneath is the drum bearing seal, not the pump (see the water-leak/anti-flood node).

leak-fill.label: Leak while filling / from a fill or inlet hose
synonyms: leak from the hose at the back
components: check the fill-hose connections at the tap and the machine (external)
discriminators: A leak only while filling, or at the rear, is usually the external fill-hose connection (at the tap or the back of the machine) - check and hand-tighten those FIRST, especially if the machine was recently moved.
If the connections are sound, the inlet valve or the internal fill hose may be leaking.

unbalanced-load.label: Unbalanced load (spin aborted / stops mid-cycle)
synonyms: keeps trying to spin then stops
discriminators: Started right after washing a single bulky, water-absorbent item (bath mat, rug, towels, duvet, blanket): that's an unbalanced load, not a fault. The item soaks up water and sticks to one side, so the machine keeps trying to redistribute and won't spin up (can look 'stuck' or 'dead' mid-cycle). Pause, open the door, redistribute or add a few smaller items, then re-run - no part needed.
Happens on EVERY load with normal mixed washing, and the machine bangs/walks: then suspect worn shock absorbers or suspension, or (with a grinding/rumbling noise) drum bearings.
Won't spin AND water is left in the drum: that's a drain fault (see not-draining), not balance.

foam-suds.label: Excess foam / suds detected
components: reduce the detergent dose / use the correct (HE) detergent
discriminators: Excess foam is almost always too much detergent or the wrong (non-HE) type - reduce the dose and run a rinse/spin to clear the suds FIRST; this is a free fix, not a part. Only if it keeps happening at the correct dose does the pressure chamber/switch (false suds/level sensing) warrant checking.
Foam pushing water out of the drawer or door is a consequence of the suds, not a failed drawer or seal.

low-voltage.label: Mains supply / voltage / frequency fault
discriminators: If it went 'dead'/stuck RIGHT AFTER washing a single bulky, water-absorbent item (bath mat, rug, towels, duvet), that's almost certainly an unbalanced load, not this - the machine is stalled trying to rebalance. Redistribute/add smaller items and re-run before suspecting a part (see unbalanced-load).

excessive-vibration.label: Bangs / bounces / walks or vibrates violently on spin
discriminators: BRAND-NEW or just-installed machine banging/bouncing from the very first spin: almost always the transit (shipping) bolts have NOT been removed - they lock the drum for transport and bypass the suspension. Remove them from the back panel (keep them for future moves), then check the machine is level with all four feet firm and lock nuts tight, and not on a springy/loose floor. No spare part needed.
An OLDER machine that has GRADUALLY started bouncing/walking: worn shock absorbers or suspension springs (bouncing), or drum bearings if there's a grinding/rumbling as the drum spins.
Only happens when washing a single bulky item (bath mat, duvet, towels): that's an unbalanced load, not worn parts - redistribute the load (see unbalanced-load).

odour.label: Smells / mouldy (maintenance)
discriminators: Usually a maintenance issue, not a fault: bacteria/detergent residue build up in the door seal folds, the drawer and the filter. Wipe out the door-seal folds, clean the filter, and run a hot 90C maintenance wash (empty) with a washing-machine cleaner or soda crystals; leave the door and drawer ajar between washes.
If a strong drain smell remains after cleaning, check the drain hose/standpipe (see not-draining).
If the rubber door seal is torn or perished and holding mould, it may need replacing.

poor-wash-results.label: Poor wash results (marks / powder left / not clean)
discriminators: Often not a fault: too much detergent, washing too cool, or overloading. Use less detergent, a hotter wash occasionally, and don't overfill.
Check water is actually flowing through the dispenser drawer and the drawer/jets aren't blocked; if little/no water reaches it, suspect the inlet valve or a blocked drawer.
Poor rinsing/marks can also follow a drainage problem (see not-draining).

damaging-clothes.label: Ripping / snagging clothes
discriminators: Most often a torn/perished door seal (boot) or a foreign object (coin, wire, bra underwire) trapped in the drum or behind the paddles - check those first.
A cracked/rough drum paddle (lifter) or a rough spot from failed drum bearings can also snag - listen for a grinding noise on spin.

tripping-electrics.label: Trips the electrics / RCD when used
discriminators: Unplug it and stop using it until fixed. On a wet appliance the classic cause is the HEATER ELEMENT going to earth (shorting) - it often trips only once the cycle reaches the heating stage. Testing/replacing the element usually fixes it.
Also check the mains cable/plug for damage and water sitting in the base; less commonly the motor or the mains suppressor/filter.
Trips the INSTANT you switch on (before any cycle) points more to the mains wiring/suppressor or the pump/motor rather than the element.

cycle-not-progressing.label: Cycle won't progress / takes hours / stuck
discriminators: If it stalls with WATER STILL IN the drum, investigate draining (filter/pump) and heating first - those commonly stall a programme. The door staying locked is a symptom of the stall, not the cause.
Note WHERE it stalls: stuck near the END/before spin with water in = a drain problem (blocked filter/pump - see not-draining).
Stuck on the wash for ages / timer counting up on a hot wash = it can't reach temperature - heater element or NTC temperature sensor.
Stuck at the START not filling (or the time keeps climbing) = not enough water - inlet valve, low pressure, or the pressure switch/level sensor.

not-draining.label: Not draining / won't empty
discriminators: If you can HEAR THE PUMP HUMMING but little water leaves, it's a drain fault (pump/filter/hose) - prioritise it over the motor; it won't spin until drained.

motor-drum.label: Motor / drum fault
discriminators: NOISE BY TIMING: noise only while DRAINING = drain pump; motor heard but drum still = belt; grinding worse at high spin = bearings; drum jerks/struggles = motor/control.

A screech/squeal on spin = drum bearings or a glazed/slipping drive belt, NOT carbon brushes. A burning-rubber smell = a slipping/perished drive belt or a seized pump/motor - unplug it if the smell is strong.

Won't spin but drains fine: this is NOT a drain fault - carbon brushes (brushed motors), a snapped/slipped drive belt, or motor control. Won't spin because water is left in the drum: it's a drain fault first (not-draining), not the motor.

CALIBRATED PRECISION: prefer a drive/motor/control AREA diagnosis unless a specific observation points to one part (grinding-worse-on-spin = bearings; motor heard, drum still = belt; drum jerks/struggles to reach speed = motor/brushes/control). Do not name an exact internal part the customer's observations cannot single out.

drying-heater.label: Drying heater fault (won't dry)
synonyms: drum cold on the drying cycle

drying-poor.label: Poor drying - airflow / filter / condenser (won't dry well)
synonyms: damp clothes after the dry cycle
discriminators: If the drum/clothes get WARM but stay damp, the heat is working - the problem is airflow or condensation: clean the lint filter AND the condenser, don't overload, and make sure the washer spun the water out first. If there is NO heat at all (drum stays cold on the drying cycle) it is a drying heater / thermal cut-out fault instead (see drying-heater).

leak-flood.label: Leak / anti-flood triggered
discriminators: A DARK, greasy/oily leak (not clear water) usually means the DRUM BEARINGS have failed - the bearing seal lets water past and dark residue out - or an oil-filled shock absorber is leaking. Listen for a grinding/rumbling on spin (bearings). Do NOT tell the customer the machine has no oil; front-loaders do have greased bearings and oil-damped absorbers. Clear-water leaks are the door seal, sump hose, pump or inlet valve.

discriminators: Started right after washing a single bulky, water-absorbent item (bath mat, rug, towels, duvet, blanket): that's an unbalanced load, not a fault. Won't spin AND water is left in the drum: that's a drain fault (see not-draining), not balance.

Remove them from the back panel (keep them for future moves), then check the machine is level with all four feet firm and lock nuts tight, and not on a springy/loose floor. No spare part needed.
An OLDER machine that has GRADUALLY started bouncing/walking: worn shock absorbers or suspension springs (bouncing), or drum bearings if there's a grinding/rumbling as the drum spins.
Only happens when washing a single bulky item (bath mat, duvet, towels): that's an unbalanced load, not worn parts - redistribute the load (see unbalanced-load).

discriminators: Unplug it and stop using it until fixed. On a wet appliance the classic cause is the HEATER ELEMENT going to earth (shorting) - it often trips only once the cycle reaches the heating stage. Testing/replacing the element usually fixes it.
Also check the mains cable/plug for damage and water sitting in the base; less commonly the motor or the mains suppressor/filter.
Trips the INSTANT you switch on (before any cycle) points more to the mains wiring/suppressor or the pump/motor rather than the element.

cycle-not-progressing.label: Cycle won't progress / takes hours / stuck
discriminators: Note WHERE it stalls: stuck near the END/before spin with water in = a drain problem (blocked filter/pump - see not-draining).
Stuck on the wash for ages / timer counting up on a hot wash = it can't reach temperature - heater element or NTC temperature sensor.
Stuck at the START not filling (or the time keeps climbing) = not enough water - inlet valve, low pressure, or the pressure switch/level sensor.

not-heating.label: Not heating / clothes stay damp
discriminators: Tumbles but stays cold: heater element or thermal cutout (a tripped cutout is often caused by a blocked lint filter/condenser - clean first).

overheating.label: Overheating / thermal cut-out
synonyms: smoke coming out of the dryer
discriminators: A burning smell from a dryer is most often lint built up on/around the heater - a FIRE RISK, so clean the lint filter and vent first. A rubbery/mechanical burning smell with a squeal or grinding is the drive belt or motor. If it also cuts out once hot, the thermostat/thermal cut-out has tripped.
Heats then cuts out / trips after a while: overheating - clean the lint filter and condenser FIRST, then suspect the thermostat/thermal cutout.

sensor.label: Moisture / temperature sensor (AutoDry) fault
discriminators: AutoDry/sensor programmes infer dryness (moisture bars in the drum, and/or temperature/humidity in the airflow - the design varies by make and architecture, so don't assume one universal sensor). Ends too early / 'dry' but damp: check programme and load first, then the moisture/temperature sensing; PCB last. Never ends / runs for hours: usually weak heat or restricted airflow (clean filter/condenser), or clothes went in soaking - not automatically the sensor or PCB.

not-emptying-condensate.label: Condensate not emptying (condenser / heat-pump dryer)
synonyms: water in the bottom of the dryer
water sitting in the bottom of my condenser dryer
water in the base of a condenser dryer
water pooling in the bottom of the dryer
dries fine but the tank never fills
clothes dry but the water tank never fills
discriminators: Condenser/heat-pump dryer, water tank fills very fast or won't fill, damp clothes: condensate pump or the float switch (check the condenser is clean).

Follow the causal water path: moisture is condensed, drops to the lower sump, the pump lifts it to the top container (or a drain hose). A 'container full/empty' warning that won't clear does NOT by itself prove the pump - check the container is seated and its detection, the float/level, and whether the sump/path is blocked with fluff-sludge. Water sitting in the base means the sump or path is blocked or the pump/hose is not moving it.

motor.label: Drum drive / motor fault (drum not turning)
synonyms: motor runs but drum doesnt turn
motor sounds like its running but drum stationary
drum hard to turn by hand
discriminators: Build the drive diagnosis in causal order: drive BELT (snapped = motor runs, drum stationary; glazed/stretched = slips), then the JOCKEY/idler tension pulley, then the MOTOR and its START CAPACITOR (hums but won't turn = capacitor), then obstruction, and only then drum support/bearings. A genuinely SEIZED drum/bearing is RARE - do not make it the default. 'Hard to turn by hand' points to support rollers/bearings; 'turns freely by hand but motor just hums' points to the capacitor or belt.

noisy.label: Noisy / abnormal noise while running
discriminators: Route dryer noise by CHARACTER, not a blanket 'noisy = motor/bearing'. Squeal/chirp (drum still turning) = jockey/idler tension pulley or a glazed belt - consider these before a motor or a seized drum. Rhythmic thump = drum support roller or a belt joint or the load. Scraping = drum support/felt or a foreign object. Rattle = blower fan or a loose object. Hum with NO drum movement = motor/start capacitor or a mechanical jam. An unusual compressor/refrigeration noise belongs to the heat-pump circuit.

fan.label: Fan / blower not working (airflow)
discriminators: The fan/blower moves hot air through the drum and out (or across the condenser). If it stops, is damaged, or is clogged with fluff you get poor drying AND overheating/thermal cut-out - so a stopped fan is a common cause behind 'overheats and cuts out'. Check it spins and is clear of lint before condemning the heater or thermostat. Airflow loss (filter, fan, duct, condenser) is a shared common cause across poor-drying, overheating and long cycles.

door.label: Door / lid switch fault
synonyms: shuts but dryer thinks its open
discriminators: A dryer that won't turn on/start: the door/lid switch must be made (door firmly shut) - a failed door switch is the usual cause. Also check the mains/fuse. If it still won't power up with the door shut, suspect the PCB (main-pcb).

Separate MECHANICAL from ELECTRICAL. A snapped handle or a door that won't physically close/latch is a mechanical part (handle/catch/hinge) - do not route a visibly broken handle to the interlock or PCB. A door that closes properly but the machine still acts 'open' points to the interlock/door switch or its wiring.

main-pcb.label: Control board / PCB fault
synonyms: random behaviour with no other symptom

heat-pump.label: Heat pump circuit underperforming
synonyms: heat pump takes longer than old vented
heat pump takes longer than my old dryer
heat pump runs cold never dries
heat pump trips after compressor starts
discriminators: A heat-pump dryer is a refrigeration system (compressor + sealed refrigerant circuit), NOT a conventional heater. It NORMALLY runs at a lower temperature and a longer programme than an old vented dryer - 'only feels warm' and 'takes longer than my old dryer' are usually NORMAL characteristics, not a fault, so do not diagnose a hardware failure from those alone. Ground a fault only on worsening performance, genuinely COLD operation that never dries, error evidence, airflow restriction, sensor behaviour, or compressor/refrigeration evidence. Never recommend a conventional heater element for a heat-pump machine.

poor-drying.label: Poor drying / takes several cycles
synonyms: takes ages to dry a load
washing comes out of the washer soaking wet and then the dryer takes forever
clothes go in soaking wet from the washer and take ages to dry
discriminators: Clean the lint filter AND the condenser/heat exchanger first - a blockage is by far the most common cause and needs no parts.
Heat-pump/condenser models: also clean the condenser and check the fluff/foam filters.
If it heats but never senses 'dry', suspect the moisture/NTC sensor; if there's no heat at all, see not-heating.

tripping-electrics.label: Trips the electrics / RCD when used
synonyms: trips as soon as it starts
discriminators: Unplug it and stop using it until fixed. On a wet appliance the classic cause is the HEATER ELEMENT going to earth (shorting) - it often trips only once the cycle reaches the heating stage. Testing/replacing the element usually fixes it.
Also check the mains cable/plug for damage and water sitting in the base; less commonly the motor or the mains suppressor/filter.
Trips the INSTANT you switch on (before any cycle) points more to the mains wiring/suppressor or the pump/motor rather than the element.

damaging-clothes.label: Tearing / snagging clothes
discriminators: A dryer that tears/snags clothes is usually a worn drum felt/rear seal (items slip into the gap) or a rough spot/crack in the drum edge.

not-draining.label: Not draining / standing water
discriminators: A dishwasher that stops mid-cycle and beeps/flashes is most often a drainage fault (blocked filter, pump or hose) - it can't pump out so it halts. Water standing in the bottom confirms it. (If it's bone dry and dead instead, look at the door switch or PCB.)
Standing water in the base that won't clear: drain pump or a blocked filter/sump; check the non-return valve.
Drains but leaves a little water each time: often normal, or a partial filter blockage.

heating.label: Heating fault (won't heat / cold wash)
synonyms: cold at the end of the cycle
discriminators: Genuine NO-HEAT (dishes and wash water clearly COLD, wash also poor, cycle may run abnormally long waiting for temperature) points to the heater / flow-through heater assembly, the NTC temperature sensor or its wiring. Many modern machines (e.g. Bosch) have NO exposed element - heating is a flow-through heater built into the circulation-pump assembly. DISHES WET BUT HOT at the end is NOT a heating fault - that is poor-drying (rinse aid / programme / plastics).

leak-flood.label: Leak / anti-flood (Aquastop) triggered
synonyms: water from the bottom of the door
leaks from the bottom of the door
water under the machine no puddle
discriminators: Water leaking FROM THE DOOR (especially the bottom) is usually the door seal/gasket, not the latch - route a door LEAK here, not to the door latch/switch fault.

door.label: Door latch / door switch fault
synonyms: nothing happens when i press start
discriminators: A dishwasher that won't turn on/start: if it still has power/lights, the usual cause is the door catch/latch not confirming the door is shut (or the on/off switch). If it's completely dead with no lights, look at the mains/PCB (main-pcb) instead.
A door that drops/slams open (rather than a latch/catch problem) is worn door balance/support springs or the hinge cables.

circulation-pump.label: Wash / circulation pump fault
discriminators: Spray arm(s) not spinning is most often a BLOCKAGE first - clean the arm jets/holes and the filter. If the arms are clear and still don't turn, it's a weak/failed wash (circulation) pump or its motor.
A loud hum/drone while WASHING usually means the wash (circulation) pump or debris caught in it; a hum only while DRAINING points to the drain pump instead.

foreign-object.label: Foreign object / debris in the sump, filter or pump
discriminators: A grinding/rattling/scraping/crunching noise (as opposed to a smooth hum) usually means a FOREIGN OBJECT - a bit of glass, a fruit stone, a bone or a piece of cutlery - has got into the sump, filter or the pump impeller. Remove the filter and clear the sump/impeller before replacing any pump; this is normally a free fix, not a spare part.
If the grinding stops after clearing the debris, no part is needed. If a spray/wash pump still hums or won't run with the sump clear, see the wash (circulation) pump.

odour.label: Smells (maintenance)
discriminators: Usually maintenance: food debris/grease in the filter and sump. Clean the filter and sump, then run a hot empty cycle with a dishwasher cleaner.
Check the drain hose isn't sitting in dirty water and standing water isn't left in the base (see not-draining).

poor-clean-results.label: Poor cleaning results (dishes dirty / gritty / filmy)
discriminators: Clean and unblock the spray arms (clear the little jet holes) and the filter first - the commonest cause of poor results.
Make sure rinse aid and dishwasher salt are topped up and the water is getting hot enough; cloudy glasses are often hard-water/rinse-aid related.
If water isn't heating or the arms aren't spinning, suspect the heater element or the wash/circulation pump.

Rusty cutlery is usually not the machine: low/empty dishwasher salt (soft water protects cutlery), a loose salt-reservoir cap letting salt into the wash, or a chipped rack coating exposing bare metal - one rusting item can mark the rest. Top up salt, check the cap, and repair/replace chipped rack tips.

foam-suds.label: Excess foam / suds (wrong detergent)
components: stop or cancel the cycle and clear the foam
discriminators: Excess foam is almost always the wrong detergent (hand dishwashing liquid) or too much detergent — not a failed pump, heater, or seal. Stop or cancel the cycle, let the foam settle, scoop or wipe it, then run an empty rinse or drain using this dishwasher's own cancel or drain control. Do not recommend a part.
Foam escaping the door is a consequence of the suds, not a failed door seal.

tripping-electrics.label: Trips the electrics / RCD when used
discriminators: Unplug it and stop using it until fixed. On a wet appliance the classic cause is the HEATER ELEMENT going to earth (shorting) - it often trips only once the cycle reaches the heating stage. Testing/replacing the element usually fixes it.
Also check the mains cable/plug for damage and water sitting in the base; less commonly the motor or the mains suppressor/filter.
Trips the INSTANT you switch on (before any cycle) points more to the mains wiring/suppressor or the pump/motor rather than the element.

spray-arm.label: Spray arm fault (blocked jets / split / not spinning)
synonyms: spray arm leaking at the door

door-loom.label: Door wiring loom / hinge flex wiring fault
synonyms: loses power when the door moves
cuts out when i move the door
works if i move the door
starts if i jiggle the door
says the door is open but it is shut

water-matrix.label: Side water matrix / heat exchanger (architecture-specific)
synonyms: big water reservoir down the side
fills with only a little water
small amount of water then weak spray
not enough water in the machine

poor-drying.label: Poor drying (dishes wet at the end)
synonyms: water droplets left on the dishes
discriminators: Dishes that are WARM/HOT but still WET at the end is NOT a heating fault - it is drying/condensation: top up the rinse aid (it sheets water off so it runs away), avoid Eco/Quick programmes that skip the heated dry, don't open the door too soon, and remember plastics naturally stay wetter than glass/ceramic. If the dishes are STONE COLD at the end (wash also poor), that is a heating fault instead (see heating).

element.label: Heating element / not heating
discriminators: Slow to reach temperature / weak heat = a partially failed element (often only glowing in parts) or a drifting oven thermostat/sensor. Uneven or one-side-only heat on a FAN oven is the fan motor instead (see uneven-heating).

Fan turning but no heat proves the fan MOTOR is working. The fan-oven element is then a strong diagnostic candidate, but it is not proven and is not automatically a purchase. Burnt wiring or connectors, the selector/function/main switch, thermostat/control path, and the supply to the element remain realistic. Distinguish a likely diagnostic component from a safe purchase recommendation.

A function that heats in one mode but not another can be the mode-specific element, OR the selector/function switch, grill energy regulator/simmerstat, thermostat/control path, wiring/connectors, or supply to that function. If the same heating system produces heat in another mode, that argues against a simple open element — it does not by itself prove the selector either. Give the discriminator (which cavity, which mode, whether it glows in grill vs heats in top-oven) and keep both directions open when remote evidence cannot tell them apart. Earth-leak behaviour belongs only when the customer reports tripping.

TOP OVEN vs GRILL (double-oven / two-cavity): the upper cavity commonly provides both top-oven cooking and grill. In top-oven mode the two element sections can be wired in SERIES so each sees roughly half mains — hot enough to cook, not necessarily glowing bright red. In grill mode the switching gives the relevant section(s) full mains so they can glow/toast. Therefore 'the element heats in top-oven mode' does not prove the complete grill function is healthy, and 'part of the grill works' does not automatically prove the element is the failed part. Compare behaviour across modes and reason about the mode-specific control/supply path as well as the element.

Engineer check order for complete no-heat (no mode producing heat): 1) the relevant element, 2) burnt element terminal connectors, 3) the selector/main switch (the commoned neutrals can burn a contact), 4) the oven thermostat (turn it and listen for the click). A function-split is not complete no-heat — do not apply this default there. Only suspect gas ignition on a GAS oven. Do not skip from a heating symptom to asking for the model to sell a part while mode, still-works, and programmer state are still open.

main-pcb.label: Control board / PCB / communication fault
discriminators: An oven/cooker that won't switch on at all, or where the clock/display and light are dead together, points to no power reaching the board - check the mains/fuse and cooker switch first, then the control board/PCB.

OVEN DEAD is ambiguous. 'My oven is dead', 'oven won't work' or 'nothing happens' is not a component diagnosis. First establish what dead means: display/clock state, whether the clock is flashing, whether fan/light works, whether any heating function works, and whether power was recently interrupted. Do not jump to the PCB or an element from the phrase alone.

A flashing clock/programmer after a power interruption is often a control-state/use-condition (the programmer left in automatic/timed mode) — not a board fault. Route that to the clock/timer advice path; do not recommend parts until manual operation has been restored or ruled out.

ignition.label: Gas ignition / flame fault
discriminators: A GAS oven/burner that lights then goes out, won't stay lit, or won't heat at all (while the grill/hob still work) is most often the FLAME FAILURE DEVICE (FSD/FFD) - the safety that shuts the gas off when it doesn't sense a flame (its thermocouple/flame probe). That mapping applies ONLY when the customer reported stay-lit / lights-then-goes-out behaviour. Uncommanded ignition sparking is not a stay-lit report. Accessing or testing the FFD/thermocouple/gas valve is for a Gas Safe engineer, not a remote DIY instruction.

thermostat.label: Thermostat fault
synonyms: cuts out after a few minutes
turns itself off after a while
shuts off when it gets hot
discriminators: Burns everything / runs too hot / food cooks too fast even on a low setting = the thermostat isn't regulating and the oven overshoots the set temperature (whole oven too hot). This is different from burning on ONE SIDE only (that's uneven-heating / the fan).

An oven that runs then cuts out after several minutes / once it's hot is usually the thermostat or a thermal overheat cut-out; on a FAN oven a failing fan motor (poor air circulation) can also trip the overheat.

selector-switch.label: Function / selector switch fault
synonyms: top oven heats grill does not
discriminators: The main/function switch on a double oven commonly performs the switching between top-oven and grill operation (series vs full-mains). Cross-mode evidence is valuable: an element that behaves one way in top-oven mode but incorrectly in grill mode should keep the MODE-SPECIFIC CONTROL/SUPPLY PATH in play as well as the element.

Do not conclude 'element works in another mode therefore the selector is faulty', and do not conclude 'grill partly heats therefore the element is faulty'. Use the complete evidence: which cavity, which mode, what still works, whether the same heating system heats in top-oven, and whether glow/toast is missing only in grill.

Grill energy regulator / simmerstat, burnt selector contacts/terminals, and wiring/connections are legitimate causes of heating-function faults. The supply/control path must remain available when evidence warrants it — this does not mean always recommending the selector.

clock-timer.label: Clock / timer / programmer state
discriminators: A flashing clock/programmer after a recent power interruption is a CONTROL-STATE / USE-CONDITION, not a parts recommendation. Many ovens default the programmer into automatic/timed operation after power loss; the oven may not heat until it is returned to MANUAL. Advise that check first. Do not surface a timer, PCB or element until manual operation has been restored or ruled out.

THIS IS ALMOST NEVER A FAULTY PART. Only if the oven still will not heat once in manual, or the clock genuinely cannot be set, is a timer/programmer component even a hypothesis — and that still is not automatically a purchase.

uneven-heating.label: Uneven heating / burning on one side
discriminators: On fan (fan-assisted) ovens the usual cause is a failing fan motor or a loose/damaged fan blade, so heat no longer circulates evenly - check the fan spins freely.
A partially failed element (visible break or only glowing in parts) or a drifting thermostat/temperature sensor can also cook unevenly.

door-glass.label: Broken / shattered door glass
discriminators: Only a CRACKED, CHIPPED, BROKEN or SHATTERED pane needs replacing. Dirt, grease, smears, marks or condensation trapped BETWEEN the panes with no crack/break is a CLEANING job (clean between the glass - see door-glass-dirty), NOT a replacement: do not recommend a replacement glass, invent breakage, or raise a shard/injury hazard for a cleaning issue.

Safety first ONLY when the glass is genuinely broken/shattered: stop using the oven and clear the glass carefully. Both the inner and outer door glass are usually replaceable parts - the exact glass is model-specific, so we need the model number.
If only the inner pane broke, the oven may still be usable briefly but should not be run until replaced.

door-glass-dirty.label: Marks or condensation trapped between the oven door glass
synonyms: clean between the oven door glass
discriminators: This is a CLEANING / access job, NOT a replacement: dirt, grease, smears, marks or condensation trapped between the door panes means the glass is intact and just needs cleaning between the layers. Do not recommend a replacement door glass, and do not tell the customer to stop using it for shards - the glass is not broken.

On most ovens the inner door glass unclips, or the door can be split, to clean between the panes (exact technique varies by make/model). Only if a pane is actually CRACKED, CHIPPED, BROKEN or SHATTERED does the glass need replacing (see broken / shattered door glass).
Persistent condensation/misting between the panes that returns after cleaning can mean a perished door seal letting moisture in - check the door seal before assuming any glass part is faulty.

lighting.label: Interior light not working
discriminators: Usually just a blown bulb - a cheap fix. Oven bulbs are special heat-resistant 300C types (often SES/E14), so use the correct one.
If a new bulb doesn't work, check the lamp holder/wiring or the door switch.

door-hinge.label: Door won't close / stay shut
discriminators: Worn or broken door hinges/springs are the usual cause of a door that won't stay shut or drops open - they're replaceable parts.
A perished door seal (gasket) can also stop the door closing flush. Give us the model and we'll find the right hinges/seal.

tripping-electrics.label: Trips the electrics / RCD when used
discriminators: An oven/cooker that trips the RCD/fuse (immediately, intermittently, or only once it is hot / after a few minutes) is often a heating element leaking to earth. Neutrals and electrical paths can be shared across grill/top, fan-oven and base elements and switched through common/main switching, so an earth-leaking element elsewhere can trip when another function is selected. The selected function is evidence, NOT proof of which element is leaking. Do not confidently recommend replacing the selected function's element from the tripping symptom alone.

Electrical insulation/leakage diagnosis is competent-person territory. Do not instruct insulation-resistance tests, megger tests, live probing, earth disconnection, RCD bypass, or repeated resets to reproduce the fault. Stop use and isolate; a qualified electrician/engineer must identify the leaking path.

door-seal.label: Oven door seal / gasket
synonyms: seal coming away from the door
discriminators: A perished/detached oven door seal (gasket) lets heat escape around the door - it's a straightforward replaceable part. (A door that won't shut/drops is the hinge; broken glass is the door glass.)

terminal-block.label: Mains terminal block / burnt supply connection
synonyms: scorched connector where the cable comes in

cooling-fan.label: Cooling fan (controls/cabinet cooling) fault
synonyms: oven cuts out when hot then works when cool
kitchen units above oven getting hot

not-cooling.label: Not cooling / warm inside
discriminators: A warm fridge with a freezer that seems cold is a COOLING-DISTRIBUTION / AIRFLOW question first, not automatic proof of a failed evaporator fan, and it does not justify listing fan + heater + PCB + timer. Ask: is cooling actually being produced (compressor running; is the freezer objectively cold — a reported 'cold freezer' is not a measured temperature)? Is cold air reaching the fridge (vents, overpacking, hidden ice on the evaporator, damper)? Is the fan known to be running or silent? Hidden ice and restricted airflow are common and often need a defrost/observation check before any part. A sealed-system failure is engineer-only.
Both compartments warm, compressor not running: compressor start relay/overload or the compressor.
Icing up at the back of the freezer: defrost system (heater/thermostat/sensor).

defrost-system.label: Defrost fault / frost build-up
synonyms: fridge warm freezer cold with ice
thick ice on the back panel
sheet of ice on the back
discriminators: Heavy/abnormal ice on the internal rear (evaporator) panel with a warm fridge but a still-cold freezer is a DEFROST-SYSTEM fault (defrost heater, defrost thermostat/thermal fuse, or defrost sensor) blocking airflow - the exact failed sub-component is model-specific, so lead with the defrost system as the area and confirm the part with the model. A manual defrost that temporarily restores cooling confirms the AREA but does not prove which sub-component failed.
Light, normal frost is not a fault; only a thick sheet/block of ice over the panel points here.

evaporator-fan.label: Internal (evaporator) fan fault
synonyms: no cold air reaching the fridge
cold air not getting to the fridge
discriminators: A warm fridge with a still-cold freezer, without a known silent fan or heavy ice, is NOT yet an evaporator-fan diagnosis. Treat it as cooling distribution: is cooling produced, is it reaching the fridge, is airflow restricted, is hidden ice plausible, is the fan actually heard or seen? Give a safe test plan (vents, listen/look for the fan, look for a sheet of ice on the rear panel, optional measured freezer temperature, a period unplugged to defrost) before naming a part. Do not dump fan + heater + PCB + timer.

FAN NOISE (rattling / knocking / grinding / buzzing) with a warm fridge and a still-cold freezer means the fan blade is striking a BUILD-UP OF ICE on the evaporator - a DEFROST-SYSTEM failure. LEAD with the defrost system (defrost heater / defrost thermostat / defrost timer) and clearing the ice; a genuinely failed fan MOTOR is usually SILENT or a steady hum, not a rattle. Only lead with the evaporator fan MOTOR when the fan is SILENT / not spinning and the coils are clear.

Warm fridge + cold freezer with NO abnormal ice and the fan silent/not spinning points to the evaporator fan motor; if there is heavy ice the fan may just be blocked by it (defrost system). Before a part, check the internal vents aren't packed with food.

fridge-airflow.label: Fridge airflow blocked (vents / overpacking) - no part
components: clear the internal air vents (usually at the back or between compartments)
move food away from the vents and the cold back wall
avoid overpacking so cold air can circulate
discriminators: A warm fridge with a still-cold freezer is often just blocked internal air vents or an overpacked compartment stopping cold air circulating from the freezer - clear the vents and rearrange the food FIRST; this is a free fix, not a part.
If the vents are clear and there is heavy ice on the rear panel, it is the defrost system; if the vents are clear, no abnormal ice and the fan is silent, it is the evaporator fan.

over-cooling.label: Fridge too cold / freezing food
discriminators: First check the thermostat/temperature dial isn't set too cold and the fridge isn't over-packed against the back vents (food touching the cold back wall freezes).
Common causes are a faulty thermostat/thermistor reading wrong, or a stuck air damper/flap letting too much cold air from the freezer into the fridge.
On frost-free models a fan/defrost airflow fault can also over-chill one area.

noisy.label: Noisy / buzzing / rattling
discriminators: A constant hum/buzz is usually the compressor or its start relay working; if it's unusually loud or the fridge isn't getting cold too, the relay or compressor may be failing.
A whirring/rattling that changes when you open the door is usually a fan (evaporator or condenser) - a blade catching ice, or a worn fan motor.
Buzzing only while it fills with water = the water inlet/ice-maker valve. A light rattle is often just pipework or a shelf touching the cabinet - reposition it (no part needed).

alarm.label: Alarm / beeping won't stop
discriminators: Most often a door-ajar or temperature alarm (by design): check both doors seal fully and nothing's blocking them, the appliance isn't over-packed with warm food, and it's had time to reach temperature.
If the doors are fine, a faulty door switch/seal or a temperature sensor reading wrong can trigger a persistent alarm - silence it per the manual once addressed.

tripping-electrics.label: Trips the electrics / RCD when running
synonyms: trips as soon as i plug it in
discriminators: A fridge-freezer that trips the RCD/fuse is an EARTH-LEAKAGE or short-circuit fault (mains lead, wiring, start relay or compressor windings), NOT a cooling-performance or refrigerant-charge question - do not lead with 'compressor failed' or 'needs re-gassing'. Timing is evidence: trips on plug-in => lead/plug/wiring or a dead short; trips when the compressor tries to start => start relay/overload or compressor windings to earth; trips after running => wiring or compressor insulation. Burning smell/scorching => STOP USE and isolate. No insulation testing, live probing, sealed-system/compressor-terminal work, earth/RCD bypass or repeated resetting by the customer.

cookware-user.label: Cookware not suitable / not detected (induction) - check the pan first
discriminators: Induction detects a pan only if the cookware is ferrous/magnetic, flat, and large enough to cover the zone - so 'won't recognise pans' is very often the COOKWARE, not the hob. Test with a magnet (it must stick firmly) and try a pan you KNOW works on the other zones. If that known-good pan also fails on this one zone, it points to the zone's coil/power (generator) module; if it works, the original pan was just unsuitable - no part needed.
A pan that is too small, warped/domed, or non-magnetic (aluminium, copper, some stainless) will not be detected on any induction zone - that is cookware, not a fault.

power-module.label: Induction power module / generator fault
discriminators: Before condemning the power/generator module, rule out the cookware: test the affected zone with a pan you KNOW heats fine on the other zones. If that known-good pan ALSO fails on this one zone (and the others still work), it's that zone's induction coil/power (generator) module. If the known-good pan works, it was just unsuitable cookware - no part needed.

overheating.label: Overheating protection triggered
discriminators: An error / 'E' shown on ALL zones at once points to a SYSTEM-WIDE cause - most commonly overheating protection (blocked vents or a failed cooling fan), or a supply / voltage problem, or the main power board - NOT a single zone's induction coil. Lead with the overheating / cooling / supply differential, do not confidently assert a dead PCB. If only ONE zone errors, that zone's coil / power module is the more likely cause.

A hob that cuts out under load, recovers when one zone is left off, or sits above an oven that is also running is a whole-hob thermal / cooling / supply path — not proof that a single zone element has failed. Unrelated co-occurring symptoms (an error code AND a separate grill fault) must not be merged into one diagnosis merely because they happened together.

The exact letter/number varies by make and generation, so an 'E' with no digits is ambiguous - give the strongest grounded differential and ask for the make/model and the full code to pin it, rather than inventing a specific meaning.

ignition.label: Gas ignition fault
discriminators: Lights then goes out when you release the knob = the flame supervision device (FSD/FFD thermocouple) isn't sensing the flame to hold the gas valve open - that's the usual culprit for 'won't stay lit'. Won't spark at all = the ignition electrode/module.

Uncommanded clicking or sparking at an electrode is an ignition/control observation. It is NOT a report of flame-failure, a thermocouple, gas smell, overheating or burning — do not invent those symptoms. Accessible burner-cap and electrode cleaning without lifting the appliance or removing panels may be customer-safe; testing or replacing gas controls, thermocouples, ignition modules, or holding the knob to test a flame-failure device is for a Gas Safe engineer. If the next useful step is inside the gas path, stop remote diagnosis there. Naming an ignition area for an engineer is not the same as instructing the customer to access or replace it.

cracked-surface.label: Cracked glass / ceramic surface
discriminators: A cracked ceramic/glass hob top is a safety and electrical risk - stop using it (moisture can reach the live elements underneath).
On most hobs the glass top isn't sold as a separate spare, so a crack usually means replacing the hob; tell us the make/model and we'll check whether a glass top is available for yours.

tripping-electrics.label: Trips the electrics / RCD when used
synonyms: trips when i turn the hob on
trips when a ring is on
discriminators: A hob that trips the RCD/fuse is an EARTH-LEAKAGE fault, but the location depends on the technology: CERAMIC/SOLID => a radiant/solid element leaking to earth or moisture/spillage tracking under the glass; INDUCTION => the coil or power module/generator or its wiring. Identify the hob type first - do not apply element reasoning to induction or module reasoning to ceramic. Timing/zone is evidence not proof; a spill/clean beforehand points to moisture - let it dry. Burning/scorching => STOP USE and isolate at the spur. No insulation testing, live probing, induction power-electronics work, earth/RCD bypass or repeated resetting by the customer.

not-heating.label: Not heating (high-voltage heating circuit)
synonyms: cuts out after a few seconds
runs then stops with no heat
discriminators: MICROWAVE TYPE DECIDES THE PRIMARY PART. On an INVERTER model (all Panasonic, and any model badged 'inverter'), a cut-out after a fixed few seconds or 'runs but no heat' is the HV INVERTER BOARD first (the magnetron is the secondary suspect) - LEAD with the inverter board. On a CONVENTIONAL (transformer) model, lead with the MAGNETRON, then the HV diode and HV capacitor.

Cuts out after a FIXED few seconds (still lit) = the power circuit isn't drawing current: inverter board (inverter models) or magnetron - this is the H97/H98 fault shown as a symptom, NOT overheating (overheating cut-outs take minutes).
Stops the instant the door is nudged: door interlock / monitor switch (see door).

CALIBRATED, SAFE PRECISION: if it starts and runs normally (turntable turning, timer counting down) but produces no heat, the fault is in the high-voltage heating circuit - describe it as a high-voltage heating-circuit fault (the exact component - magnetron, HV diode, HV capacitor or inverter board - depends on the model and can only be confirmed by an engineer's test), do NOT name a single failed part or claim it is 'the magnetron'. NEVER tell the customer to remove the cover/casing, discharge the capacitor, or test the magnetron/diode/transformer - dangerous voltage can remain stored even when unplugged; this is an engineer diagnosis, not a DIY test.

SAFE DISCRIMINATOR FIRST: if it is unclear whether it runs normally or won't start / reacts to the door, ask that (runs-normally-but-cold vs won't-start / door-conditioned) before committing - a door/latch/interlock fault stops it heating too, and is a completely different (and often no-HV) repair (see door).

cutting-out.label: Overheats / cuts out after several minutes
synonyms: turns off mid cycle after minutes
discriminators: This node is for cut-outs after MINUTES of running (thermal overheat / cooling fan). A cut-out after a FIXED FEW SECONDS is NOT overheating - suspect the magnetron/inverter power circuit (not-heating) or a door interlock/monitor switch instead.
Cuts out only after several MINUTES, often warm with a hot smell: overheating - failing cooling fan, blocked vents, or a tripped thermal cutout.
Cuts out after a FIXED few SECONDS instead: that is NOT overheating - on an inverter (Panasonic) it is the inverter board/magnetron; see not-heating.

noisy.label: Noisy / loud when running
discriminators: A grinding/whirring from underneath as the plate turns = the turntable motor; a loud rushing/rattle = the cooling fan or a loose cover.
A loud HUM or buzz together with poor/no heating points to the magnetron or HV components on their way out (see not-heating).

lost-suction.label: Lost suction / poor pickup
discriminators: First clear blockages: check the hose, wand and floor head for clogs, and empty the bin or replace the dust bag.
Wash or replace the filters (a clogged HEPA/pre-motor filter is the commonest cause of gradual suction loss).
Check the hose for splits and that all seals/lids are seated - a small air leak kills suction.

brush-bar.label: Brush bar / roller not spinning
discriminators: Usually a snapped/stretched drive belt (cheap, common) or the brush bar jammed with hair and threads - cut the tangle away and spin it by hand.
If the belt and brush are fine, the brush-bar motor (on powered floor heads) may have failed.

Suction still present with a dead brush/roller is a brush-drive / floor-head / settings path, not a failed suction motor. Check the floor-head setting and the brush belt before condemning the main motor or battery.

wont-run.label: Won't switch on / no power
synonyms: nothing happens when i press the button
discriminators: A vacuum that is TOTALLY DEAD (no lights, nothing) points to the power supply: on a corded model check the cable, plug fuse and on/off switch; on a cordless model check the battery and charger first (a flat or failed battery is the usual culprit, and many show a flashing charge light).
If it powers up but then stops shortly after, that is a cut-out (overheat or a cordless blockage/battery protection), not a no-power fault - see cuts out / stops after running.
Only suspect the motor once the cable, switch, battery and charger are ruled out.

cuts-out.label: Cuts out / stops after running (overheat or battery protection)
synonyms: turns itself off after a while
components: blockage in the hose or airway
discriminators: Cutting out after a short run is nearly always overheating from a blocked pre-motor filter or a blockage in the hose/airway tripping the thermal cut-out - clean/replace the filters and clear any blockage, then let it cool before trying again.

On a CORDLESS machine a flashing light that stops the motor after a few seconds is usually the battery or blockage-protection cutting in - check for a blockage and that the battery is charged before suspecting a part.
A cut-out after MINUTES with the body hot is overheating/airflow; a totally dead machine that never starts is a power fault instead (see won't switch on).

motor.label: Motor fault (worn or failed motor)
discriminators: A genuinely failed motor usually sounds rough - a screech, roar, grind or loud whine - or has worn carbon brushes; before condemning the motor, clean the filters and clear any blockage, as a restricted airway overheats and stresses the motor.
A machine that is totally dead is more likely a power/switch/battery fault than the motor (see won't switch on).

hotpoint-indesit._note: Legacy F-code system. Meanings differ across EVO-I / EVO-II / Arcadia platforms AND between washing machines, washer-dryers and dishwashers, so the SAME F-number can mean different things. High-numbered codes (F10+) are especially platform-dependent. WM F06 mapped to door-lock per iFixit (some Ariston boards use F06 as a keypad/button fault). WM F15 mapped to leak-flood per Glotech Indesit list (conflicts with some 'drain' interpretations). Dishwasher F15 mapped to turbidity/visual sensor per JustFixed (Glotech lists an F15 flood variant on some models). Older Ariston/Hotpoint FDW dishwashers use AL / A-codes instead of F-codes (A04/A05 included). Verify per platform. Older EVO-I models flash an LED instead of a display; flash-count = F-code number (captured as FLASHn).

bsh._note: BSH Hausgeraete shared platform. On washing machines the E-prefix and F-prefix versions of the same number are equivalent (E17 = F17). Codes below are the main modern WAE/WAS/WOK/WOL platform; older WFF/WFL/WFP ranges use a DIFFERENT F-code meaning set (not mapped here) — verify the range first. Dishwasher codes shown are the modern E:xx set (also seen as plain Exx). Oven/hob E-codes vary by model; E305 is mapped to a control-board/communication fault per BSH support pages but some third-party lists call E305 a cavity-sensor fault — treat oven codes as low-confidence.

beko._note: Arcelik shared platform (Beko/Blomberg/Grundig/Leisure/Flavel). WM E-codes are consumer-facing; H-codes are engineer service-mode diagnostics (included, mapped to the same faults at component level). WM E01 is normally a door-lock fault but some models use E1 for an NTC fault — check the H-code where available. Beko NTC reads ~4.7k ohm (differs from ~30k on other brands). Dishwasher E01 is an overflow/leak (shown as a 'P1' icon on bar-display models). Tumble-dryer E1 = NTC/thermistor sensor per third-party lists (low confidence, condenser vs vented models differ).

whirlpool._note: Whirlpool AWO/AWD/EU front-loaders use letter codes (FH/FA/FP) alongside numbered F-codes; the Dreamspace range uses numbered F-codes with some differing meanings. Whirlpool owned Hotpoint/Indesit 2014-2024, so shared-platform models often mirror the Hotpoint F-code set — cross-check the hotpoint-indesit family. Dishwasher mapping is limited to the two codes reliably documented on Whirlpool's own LED-interface service page (F02 fill, F03 drain); other dishwasher codes were omitted pending confirmation.

hoover-candy._note: Both owned by Haier Europe and share the 'Cuore' control board; E-codes are largely interchangeable BUT meanings diverge between collector-motor (older) and induction-motor (newer, brushless) models — on induction models a motor code points to the speed sensor/inverter board, not carbon brushes. Mapping below follows the Candy code set as primary; Hoover's own advice pages describe some codes differently (e.g. E04 as over-dosing/water container on some Hoover models vs NTC on the whitegoodshelp Hoover list) — verify per model and motor type. E17 mapped to hall-sensor for induction models. Washer-dryer drying codes (E11/E15) mapped under washer-dryer.

electrolux-aeg._note: Electrolux AB shared platform (AEG Lavamat / Electrolux / Zanussi) — codes and parts are effectively identical across the three brands. WM codes use a grouped Exx structure: E1x fill, E2x drain, E3x pressure/level, E4x door, E5x motor, E6x heating, E7x NTC, E9x board/comms, EF0 anti-flood/foam. Some E30/E31 codes are door-lock on certain models rather than pressure — verify. E52 is most commonly worn carbon brushes on collector-motor models over ~5 years. Electrolux-group dishwashers use a separate i-code system (i10 fill, i20 drain, i30 leak/aqua-control tray, i40 pressure sensor, i50 wash/circulation motor, i60 heating, i70 NTC, i90 software config, iB0 turbidity sensor, iC0 UI comms, iD0 no tacho signal, iE0 diverter valve, iF0 overfill); on display-less models the same faults appear as flashing counts and older AL5/AL6/C1/C2/F1/F2 aliases.

samsung._note: Modern Samsung uses two-character codes where the E and C letter variants mean the same fault (5E = 5C). Older Samsung machines use E-number codes (E1-E7) that map to the modern set (cross-reference included). Samsung uses brushless Digital Inverter (direct-drive) motors on most models — motor codes (3E/SE) point to the hall sensor, NOT carbon brushes. OE = overflow (mapped to inlet-valve as the usual overfill cause). CE on washer-dryers is a cooling/over-temperature fault (mapped under washer-dryer). Dishwasher 1C is a low-water/drain-sensor condition (mapped to fill).

lg._note: LG uses Direct Drive (brushless) motors on the vast majority of machines — there are NO carbon brushes, so motor codes (LE/SE/CE) point to the hall/rotor-position sensor, the inverter board, overload, or a drum obstruction. LE = motor locked, most often simple overloading; mapped to motor-current. CL (child lock), tCL (tub clean) and PF (power failure) are informational, not faults (PF mapped to low-voltage; CL/tCL omitted). Older E-number codes map to the two-letter set. LG dishwasher codes were not confidently sourced and are omitted pending research.

miele._note: Miele F-codes. F53 is documented as a motor speed-sensor fault on some sources and a motor/carbon-brush fault on others (mapped to tacho — verify motor type, as many Miele machines are brushless). F01/F02 are NTC short/open; F10 = water inlet blocked/restricted (mapped to inlet-valve); F11 = drain restricted (check filter first); F138 = water in the floor tray (leak). Dishwasher: F11 = drain fault with water in the cabinet; F70 = waterproof/float ('Waterproof System') triggered (leak). Older vs newer generations (W1 etc.) differ — verify per model.

smeg._note: Smeg appliances are often OEM-built; codes vary by model/platform.

haier._note: Haier washing-machine ERR/E codes vary by model.

hisense._note: Limited public code data; often shares platforms with other far-east OEMs. before trusting codes.

fisher-paykel._note: F&P use numeric fault/beep codes that are model-specific; not enumerated here. — diagnose by symptom.

rangemaster._note: Range cookers/ovens (AGA group). Limited public codes; diagnose by symptom..

cda._note: CDA is a reseller — appliances are OEM rebadges (platforms vary, e.g. Beko/Vestel). Check the underlying platform..

servis._note: Servis (now Vestel-owned) rebadges — codes follow the underlying Vestel/other platform..

montpellier._note: Montpellier is a reseller — OEM rebadges. Check the underlying platform..

gorenje._note: Gorenje WM F-code set per service manual 4-022-0412: F1 temp-sensor open/short, F2 door-lock open connection, F3 water level not reached (fill), F4 tacho open/short, F5 triac short, F6 temperature not reached (heat), F7 water level won't fall (drain), F8 max spin not reached. Meanings vary by generation — verify per model.

daewoo._note: Daewoo two-letter set: IE inlet, OE/QE/PFE drain, UE unbalance, LE/dE/SE door/lid, E2 overflow, E4 leak, E5/E6 motor DC-link/overcurrent, E7 hall/direction, E8 motor, E9 pressure sensor, H2/H5 thermistor, H4/H8 overheat, H6 heater. Meanings vary by platform (DWD-F vs DWC) — verify.

panasonic._note: Panasonic uses U- (user) and H- (hardware) prefixes. U04/U12/U13 = control-module/program, U14 = supply voltage, U18 = sensor comms. H01/H05/H09/H29/H41/H52 = control board, H27/H53 = door/supply/drain blocked (mapped to door-lock as primary), H43/H46/H51/H55 = tacho/motor. Meanings vary by model — verify.

_displayTypes: Codes may be: alphanumeric (e.g. F03, E15, i20, 4C), letter (OE, UE), or blink-pattern (FLASHn = n LED flashes on legacy no-display models).

_generic.reset: Switch it off at the wall (or unplug) for about 5-10 minutes so the electronics fully discharge, then power back on. This clears many one-off error codes, especially after you've fixed the cause (e.g. cleared a blocked filter). To cancel a stuck program first, hold Start/Pause for a few seconds.
_generic.testMode: Most machines have an engineer diagnostic/test mode entered with a button combination as you switch on; it steps through fill, heat, wash, drain and spin to test each part. The exact keys vary by model, so check that model's manual. It will actually run water, heating and spin, so only use it with the machine empty.

bsh.reset: Bosch/Siemens/Neff have no button-combo reset - turn it off at the wall for 5-10 minutes to discharge, then power back on. Hold On/Off (or Start) to stop a running program. If a control-board code like E63/F63 returns after a reset, the fault is still present and needs looking at.
bsh.testMode: There is a service/test program, but the entry combo differs across models (often holding a program button while switching on) - check the specific model's manual. It runs the machine through its stages, so keep it empty.

hotpoint-indesit.reset: Turn it off at the wall for a few minutes and back on; to cancel a program hold Start/Pause for about 5 seconds. A power cycle clears many transient codes once you've dealt with the cause.
hotpoint-indesit.testMode: On many Hotpoint/Indesit models you reach the test/diagnostic mode by pressing so both the Start and Cancel buttons are held together until the display shows a test indication (e.g. a 'd' or TEST), then use Start to step through the checks. It runs the machine, so keep it empty. Exact behaviour varies by model.

beko.reset: Power-cycle at the wall for a few minutes, then back on; hold Start/Pause a few seconds to cancel a program. Beko H-codes are engineer diagnostics - a reset clears the display but not an underlying fault.
beko.testMode: Beko engineer test mode is model-specific (typically a program-dial position combined with holding Start) - check the model's service info. It runs the machine through its stages.

electrolux-aeg.reset: Turn off at the wall for a few minutes then on; hold Start to cancel a program. Clears transient E-codes once the cause is fixed.
electrolux-aeg.testMode: AEG/Electrolux/Zanussi diagnostic mode is engineer-level (on many EWM control boards you hold two program buttons while turning the dial to enter it) and varies by platform - check the model's service manual. It cycles through component tests.

samsung.reset: There's no true reset - switch it off at the wall (or breaker) for 1-5 minutes to discharge, then power back on and restart the cycle.
samsung.testMode: Samsung has a 'Smart Check' self-diagnosis: with the machine on, press and hold the two indicated buttons together (varies by model, often the Temperature / Water-level pair) for about 3 seconds to show a check code you can look up in the Samsung app. Front-loaders also have a test mode (hold Delay Start plus a Soil-level button). Keep it empty as it will run the machine.

lg.reset: Unplug (or breaker off) for 1-2 minutes then power back on; on some models, with the power off, hold Start/Pause for 5 seconds. Clears many one-off codes.
lg.testMode: LG has a quick test: with the machine on, press and hold the Spin and Soil buttons together until a test code appears, then press Start - it runs a short (~3 minute) check of the water inlet and drain. LG Smart Diagnosis can also send data to their app. Keep the drum empty.

whirlpool.reset: Power-cycle at the wall; on dial models, turning the dial one full turn anticlockwise from a start position resets it. Hold Pause/Cancel to clear the display.
whirlpool.testMode: Whirlpool service diagnostic: with the machine in standby (plugged in, all lights off), within 8 seconds press and release the same three buttons in order, repeating that 3-button sequence three times - all indicators light to confirm, then you can step through the component tests. Keep it empty.

hoover-candy.reset: Turn the dial to off/reset and power-cycle at the wall for a few minutes. A child-lock (which can block starting) is usually toggled by holding two buttons for ~2 seconds - look for the key symbol on the panel.
hoover-candy.testMode: Many Hoover/Candy models start a self-test when you hold Start/Pause from a set dial position - the exact combo varies by model, so check its manual. It runs through the wash stages.

platforms.panasonic: Panasonic microwaves are INVERTER models (no HV transformer). Running then cutting out after a FIXED few seconds (still lit) with little/no heat = the power circuit not drawing current (same fault as H97/H98) - NOT overheating (overheating cut-outs take minutes). On Panasonic the HV INVERTER BOARD is the PRIMARY suspect - LEAD with the inverter board; the magnetron is the secondary suspect. Do NOT lead with the magnetron on a Panasonic.
platforms.lg: LG uses Direct Drive (brushless) motors - there are NO carbon brushes. Motor/spin faults point to the hall/rotor-position sensor, the inverter/main PCB, or a drum obstruction.
platforms.samsung: Samsung uses Digital Inverter (direct-drive) motors - motor faults point to the hall sensor / PCB, not carbon brushes. E and C letter code variants mean the same fault.
platforms.bsh: Bosch/Siemens/Neff share the BSH platform; the E- and F-prefixed versions of the same washing-machine number are equivalent (E17 = F17).
platforms.beko: Beko/Arcelik: E-codes are consumer-facing, H-codes are engineer service codes for the same faults. NTC sensor reads ~4.7k ohm (vs ~30k on many other brands).
platforms.hotpoint-indesit: Hotpoint/Indesit legacy F-codes vary by control platform (EVO-I / EVO-II / Arcadia); the SAME F-number can mean different things across washing machines, dryers and dishwashers.
platforms.miele: Many Miele machines are brushless - a 'motor' fault often means the speed/tacho sensor, not carbon brushes.
platforms.whirlpool: Whirlpool owned Hotpoint/Indesit 2014-2024, so shared-platform models often mirror the Hotpoint F-code set.
platforms.electrolux-aeg: AEG/Electrolux/Zanussi share a platform; washing-machine codes use a grouped Exx scheme (E1x fill, E2x drain, E3x pressure/level, E4x door, E5x motor, E6x heat, E7x NTC, E9x board).
platforms.hoover-candy: Hoover/Candy share the Cuore board; on newer induction (brushless) motors a motor code points to the speed sensor/inverter, not carbon brushes.

washing-machine: around the door opening (on the rim, visible with the door open)
washer-dryer: around the door opening (on the rim)
tumble-dryer: on the rear or side rating plate
dishwasher: on the edge of the door (side or top, visible when the door is open)
fridge-freezer: on a label inside the fridge compartment (often on a side wall or near the salad drawer)
sometimes behind the bottom kick-plate or on the rear
oven-cooker: around the door frame (open the door and look around the opening)
on the rear (may need to pull it out)
hobs: on the underside of the hob
sometimes on a rear rating plate
vacuum: on the base or body of the machine
